articles.title: ‘My Sad Dead’ Review: An Urban Community Gets the Haunting It Deserves in Pablo Larraín’s Superb Modern Gothic
articles.summary: Macabre and melancholy but suffused with a delicious absurdism that somehow doesn’t clog the arteries of its hopeful little heart, Pablo Larraín’s sprawling, peculiar, terrific “My Sad Dead” is about 20 things at once in every moment. It’s a ghost story, obviously, on account of all the ghosts.
body: A doctor who can see the dead becomes the reluctant guardian to a Buenos Aires neighborhood plagued by violence in a dolorous but darkly witty grotesque based on Mariana Enriquez's short stories.

It’s not her, exactly, but a fuzzy, not-quite-opaque facsimile of her. The effect that “My Sad Dead” uses to summon the dead is the more convincing for not being particularly flashy. The unusual, low-contrast color palette that Larraín and his ace regular DP Sergio Armstrong have chosen blanches the images to a flat, pinkish gray, so that those with and without heartbeats all have the pallor of a mortuary waiting room’s magnolia walls.

articles.title: ‘NAZA’ Co-Director Yuval Abraham Calls Out the U.S. Government for ‘Funding’ Israel’s Destruction of Gaza, Telling NYFF Audience: ‘This Is What Your Country Is Supporting’
articles.summary: The Gaza documentary “NAZA” made its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival to a massive standing ovation for co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor who gave a brief Q&A with festival director Dennis Lim after the screening.
body: “NAZA” first premiered at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, where it won a special jury prize and received a record-breaking 24.5-minute standing ovation. The documentary was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv and shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.” It is now set to release in more than 50 territories before becoming available to stream for free on The Guardian’s website.

Since its premiere, the directors have come under fire from a number of Israeli officials — Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for the introduction of a law that would “revoke the citizenship of anyone who slanders IDF [Israeli Defense Forces] soldiers” following the film’s debut, while Israel’s Minister of Culture threatened to revoke the filmmaker’s Israeli citizenship.

articles.title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Spoofs Oasis as Russian Hackers Who Trick Prime Minister Andy Burnham by Asking Him to Join the Band
articles.summary: Oasis and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were at the heart of a surreal cold open in the third episode of “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Season 2, where the iconic Manchester-based duo turned out to be a Russian psyop stealing Burnham’s personal details.
body: “I tell you what, you absolutely smashed that speech to the UN,” Rayner responded. “About time someone stood up to Russia. They hate us because we have freedom and Greggs.”
“I’m sick of Russia trying to divide us people,” Burnham said. “We can divide ourselves, thank you very much.”

Liam (Jack Shep) and Noel Gallagher (Freddie Meredith) from Oasis then appeared and asked Burnham whether he could fill in for Liam playing the guitar at their next gig due to an injury. Burnham agreed and was asked to hand over his personal details, to which he gleefully agreed. Almost immediately, Noel and Liam Gallagher started donning Russian accents..

With the threat that the U.K. will now become a Russian puppet state, Burnham does not give in. “Just because you have the power to do something, doesn’t mean you should. I, for example, could hold a general election tomorrow and easily smash it,” Andy said. “But as I announced yesterday, I won’t do. And I could. Maybe I should. And I will. But I won’t. Unless I do. Which I won’t. Unless I do. And that is true leadership.”

articles.title: Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ Sweeps San Sebastian Awards as ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘NAZA’ Earn Audience Nods
articles.summary: Amanda Kernell's 'Brace Your Heart' won the Swedish-Sami filmmaker the Silver Shell for best director as the Spanish film fest wrapped up its 74th edition, the last for outgoing director Jose Luis Rebordinos.
body: Mike Leigh ’s dramatic comedy Tender Loving Care took home three top awards at Saturday night’s closing ceremony of the 74th annual edition of the San Sebastian International Film Festival, which ran Sept. 18-26, including the Golden Shell for best film and Silver Shell for Kate O’Flynn’s lead performance.
O’Flynn shared the award with Asta Kamma August for her work in Hans Petter Moland’s Growth of the Soil, which also took home best cinematography for DP Oskar Dahlsbakken.

The Silver Shell for best director went to Sweden’s Amanda Kernell for Brace Your Heart. She dedicated the prize to members of the Sami culture represented in her film about reindeer herders, a “living culture facing immense stress.” She highlighted “the importance that films can give voice to those without a voice and be this machine of empathy.”
The Special Jury Prize went to Ah Biao’s Border. Spain ’s Javier Cámara took home the Silver Shell for best supporting performance in Javier Ruiz Caldera’s 5 More Minutes.

articles.title: Robert Vaughn Played A Small Part In One Of The Worst Superhero Movies Ever Made
articles.summary: While his role on The Man from U.N.C.L.E. brought Robert Vaughn great success, the same cannot be said for his turn in this superhero movie misfire.
body: Everyone knows Robert Vaughn as the suave secret agent Napoleon Solo from the 1960s NBC series "The Man from U.N.C.L.E." But in 1983, he played the kind of villain Solo would have taken down with a wry smile and a cool insouciance. Indeed, the actor's character, Ross Webster, was a scheming industrialist who faced off against the Man of Steel in 1983's "Superman III." In retrospect, Vaughn probably would have preferred for Webster to be a quickly forgotten villain on his spy series, though, as "Superman III" turned out to be a bit of a dud, and that's putting it lightly.

articles.title: Quentin Tarantino Fans Will Love This Brilliant, Criminally Underseen Thriller
articles.summary: If you enjoy the films of Quentin Tarantino and are looking for something with a similar flavor, check out this excellent underseen thriller.
body: Are you a fan of the films of Quentin Tarantino? More specifically, do you vibe with his single-room thrillers like "Reservoir Dogs" and "The Hateful Eight?" If that sounds like you, then hop on over to Hoopla, The Roku Channel, or YouTube and check out Henry Dunham's "The Standoff at Sparrow Creek," a provocative tension-boiler about some very unsavory characters.

"The Standoff at Sparrow Creek" is a nail-biting thriller that locks a group of questionable men in a warehouse and keeps turning up the temperature. The story centers around militia members who discover that an AR-15 is missing from their gun cabinet. The problem with that? Earlier that day, a gunman shot up a nearby police officer's funeral with the same weapon. As such, it's only a matter of time until the law comes after them, forcing Gannon (James Badge Dale) — a former cop — to interrogate everyone and flush out the shooter.
points: If you enjoy the films of Quentin Tarantino and are looking for something with a similar flavor, check out this excellent underseen thriller.

articles.title: Viral Lesbian Bar Article From Boston Globe Is Piquing Hollywood’s Interest
articles.summary: The article has spurred thousands of subscriptions to the paper. Now UTA, which reps the Globe, is fielding inquiries about adaptations.
body: In the early 2000s, The Boston Globe published a series of bombshell articles that exposed the cover-up of abuse within the Catholic Archdiocese of Boston. The series was one of the more consequential pieces of journalism this century, winning a Pulitzer Prize and inspiring Spotlight, the 2015 film that won a best picture Oscar.
The Sept. 22 article by Annalisa Quinn was all over social media feeds this week and quickly became one of the most read stories in Globe history.
Now, insiders tell THR that UTA, which represents the Globe, has been fielding inquiries about potential adaptations for the article — both in the scripted space and the documentary sphere.

Indeed, the article has several ready-made characters, from a besieged bar owner drowning in debt to former patrons furious that the bar has killed its mask policy — and who go above and beyond to let the owner know what they think.
